source_refs.note: Topic 5.9, printed pages 106-107, as printed, with Figure 5.9 (original drawing). The print's 'Table (5.9)' is marked; it is Table 5.4.

blocks.text: When a liquid is heated, its vapour pressure goes on increasing. A stage reaches when the vapour pressure of the liquid becomes equal to the atmospheric or external pressure. At this temperature the liquid starts boiling. The reason for this is that the bubbles of vapour which are formed in the interior of the liquid have greater internal pressure than atmospheric pressure on the surface of liquid. This makes the bubbles to come out of the liquid and burst at the surface. A constant stream of bubbles comes out at the boiling point of the liquid.

blocks.alt: A graph of vapour pressure (0 to 800 torr) against temperature (0 to 120 degrees C) for four liquids. Each curve rises steeply. Diethyl ether reaches 760 torr, and boils, at 34.6 C, ethanol at 78.3 C and water at 100 C; ethylene glycol's curve stays near the axis because it boils far above 100 C.
blocks.caption: Vapour pressures (torr) of four common liquids against temperature (original diagram after Figure 5.9).

blocks.text: When a liquid is heated, the kinetic energy of its molecules increases. This causes the increase of the temperature. At the boiling point, the kinetic energy of the molecules becomes maximum. Any further heating at this stage will not increase the temperature. This further heating is utilized to break the intermolecular forces and convert the liquid into its vapour. The boiling points of some commonly available liquids at one atmospheric pressure are shown in the Table (5.9).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed reference “Table (5.9)” should read Table 5.4 (Boiling points of some common liquids at 760 torr), printed in 5.9.1.

The Figure 5.9 shows the variation of vapour pressure of water, ethyl alcohol, ethylene glycol and diethyl ether with temperature. The graphs show that the liquids reach upto their boiling points when their vapour pressures are equal to 760 torr at sea level.
